data.body:
Evidence from another session, not a decision on this epic — I do not own it and am not claiming it. Recording a measurement and one observed failure that bear on its urgency, so the owner has them.

**Observed today (2026-09-05 08:42 UTC).** Gerrit change 2670 took `Verified -1` from the `require resolvable rebar ticket` job. The job never reached ticket resolution: it died fetching the tickets branch from GitHub.

    error: RPC failed; HTTP 408 curl 22 The requested URL returned error: 408
    ##[error]Process completed with exit code 128
    (after 3 attempts)

The change itself was fine — trailer `rebar-ticket: affd-913c-3fb0-40fb`, resolving locally via `rebar verify-commit-ticket --rev HEAD`, ticket present on `origin/tickets`. I posted a `recheck` citing the environmental fault, and CI restarted cleanly.

**Current size, measured:** `origin/tickets` now carries **254,111 commits across 198,444 files**.

**Why this belongs on THIS epic rather than as a new bug.** The pack-size ceiling that used to make this growth visible was deliberately REMOVED — closed ticket `bardic-continuous-asianlion` records the pack at 131,830 KiB against a 131,072 KiB limit on 2026-08-04, and the chosen fix was to delete the `REBAR_TICKETS_PACK_LIMIT_KIB` gate outright rather than raise it, on the reasoning that a fixed ceiling against append-only monotonic growth is guaranteed to keep tripping repo-wide. That was a defensible call, and its own note said bounding the growth "would need a real mechanism (server-side gc / history compaction)" — which is this epic.

The consequence worth flagging is a change in FAILURE SHAPE, not just magnitude. With the ceiling in place, growth announced itself as a legible `Verified -1` naming a KiB number. With it gone, the same growth now surfaces as an HTTP 408 on a per-change fetch — indistinguishable at a glance from an ordinary network flake, on a job whose NAME ("require resolvable rebar ticket") points at the change's trailer rather than at the store. I nearly mis-attributed it to the trailer myself before reading the log.

**What I did NOT establish, stated plainly so this is not over-read.** One occurrence is not a trend. I checked the three preceding failed runs (33954406874, 33953469347, 33951134881) and all three failed on pytest jobs, not this one. So I have a single 408, and the size figure raises its prior probability without demonstrating causation. If someone wants to settle it, the discriminating measurement is fetch DURATION for this job over time — a rising duration approaching the server's timeout is the signal; a single timeout is not.

No action taken on this epic and none proposed. Purely evidence.
